newsitem.title: INDIA: India stocks sizzle to 20-mth highs, tops in Asia.
newsitem.headline: India stocks sizzle to 20-mth highs, tops in Asia.

text.p: A sizzling 38 percent rally in the first half of 1997, largely led by foreign fund buying, has made Indian stock exchanges the best performers in Asia this year, analysts said on Tuesday.

The benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange 30-share index surged 1,171 points, or 38 percent, to 4,256.09 in the first half of 1997 -- beating China's gains of 37 percent, Taiwan's 30.2 percent and Hong Kong's 13 percent in the same period, they said.
In late afternoon trade on Tuesday the Bombay index was up 45.64 points at 4,301.73.
V.V. Sivakumar, head of research at Peregrine Capital said India has been the top performing market in Asia.
"The outlook is still positive. The markets are still to run their full course ... it's just that the pace may wary. We are maintaining our year-end target of 4,500," he said.
Other analysts said the outlook was bullish based on falling interest rates, triggered by cuts last week in major banks' prime lending rates to 13.5 percent -- the lowest in more than two years.
"The market is awash with liquidity," K.R. Bharat, country head at Credit Suisse First Boston told Reuters. "There is so much money going into the system."

Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) have been the biggest buyers during the market's bull run, with net FII investment between June 1 and June 24 totalling 10.84 billion rupees ($302.6 million), unofficial figures show.
Net foreign institutional investment inflows in May were $198.4 million and $148.5 million in April, according to Securities & Exchange Board of India figures.
"There are also increasing allocations made to India because of problems in other Asian markets such as Thailand," Credit Suisse's Bharat said.

"The real issue is that if fund managers have enough money and India seems to be relatively attractive, where else does one put the money?" asked the head of dealing at a European securities firm who did not want to be identified.
Despite the sharp rally seen this year, the markets could consolidate before making the next upward charge, fund managers said.

"A 10 percent rise from these levels looks feasible. There are hopes of an economic turnaround, clearly, we have to look ahead," said Gul Tekchandani, chief investment officer at Sun Foreign & Colonial Asset Management.
"We should see a lot of volatility."

Market participants said they were convinced about an uptrend in industrial production in 1997/98 (April-March) based on falling interest rates, increased bank credit, lower corporate taxes and stable agricultural growth.

"We are fairly positive even from here on, but the only concern is that the economic numbers coming out are not very positive yet," said Neeraj Roy, head of institutional sales at Bombay-based Prime Securities.
India's index of industrial growth rose by 6.7 percent in the year to March 1997 compared to a 11.6 percent rise in the same period in 1996, government figures show.
Several manufacturing sectors showed a downtrend in 1996/97 due to tight credit, heavy inventories and slack demand.

"The fact that people do not want to put money in financial assets such as fixed deposits and debt instruments ....means that either you consume that money or go ahead and put it in equities," the dealing head at the foreign firm said.
Government steps to improve economic fundamentals would determine any follow-up buying, fund managers said.
"I think the rally still has some steam left. Further upside trends depend on whether the problems on the macro-economic front are dealt with," said Credit Suisse's Bharat.
"If we get quick solutions by the government in terms of the fiscal deficit, the oil pool deficit and infrastructure problems -- these will show if the rally can be sustained."
